name: The Gaia Hypothesis
statement: Life and its environment form one self-regulating system that keeps the Earth fit for life.
meaning: The Gaia hypothesis proposes that living organisms interact with their inorganic surroundings on Earth to form a synergistic, self-regulating, complex system that helps maintain and perpetuate the conditions for life on the planet. On this view, biological and physical processes are coupled through feedback loops that hold key planetary variables, global temperature, atmospheric composition, ocean salinity, within ranges tolerable for life. It ranges from a weak, widely accepted reading, that life significantly influences its environment, to a strong, rejected version in which the biosphere behaves almost purposefully.
mechanism: Life and environment are coupled by feedbacks, some stabilising and some not. James Lovelock's insight, developed with the microbiologist Lynn Margulis, was that Earth's atmosphere is biologically transformed and held far from chemical equilibrium by living processes. The credible, non-teleological mechanism is that ordinary natural selection and physics can produce planet-scale regulation without foresight. The Daisyworld model, by Lovelock and Andrew Watson, made this concrete: an imaginary planet of light and dark daisies, each simply maximising its own growth, passively regulates temperature as its star brightens, showing self-regulation can emerge from local competition alone.

examples.text: Lovelock and Watson's model planet of black and white daisies keeps its temperature near the optimum as the star brightens, purely through Darwinian competition, with no planning or purpose.
Oxygen has stayed near twenty-one percent and ocean salinity near three and a half percent over long timescales, constancies Gaia proponents cite as suggestive of biological regulation.

examples.tag: Weathering and the faint young Sun
examples.text: Life-mediated weathering and carbon drawdown are offered as part of why Earth stayed habitable even as the young Sun was far fainter, though a non-biological silicate thermostat is the mainstream account.

variants.name: Weak to strong Gaia
variants.text: A spectrum from influential and coevolutionary Gaia, that life shapes its environment, through homeostatic Gaia, that the coupling is stabilising, up to the optimising, teleological version that is widely rejected.

variants.name: The Medea counter-hypothesis
variants.text: Peter Ward's explicit anti-Gaia, that multicellular life is ultimately self-destructive, offered as the named counterpoint to Gaian optimism.

whyItMatters: Gaia was a major intellectual driver behind treating the Earth as a single coupled system rather than as separate geology, biology, atmosphere, and oceans, a framing that underlies modern Earth system science. It foregrounded how far life shapes global chemical cycles, and Lovelock's original insight, that a living planet betrays itself through atmospheric chemical disequilibrium, remains directly relevant to the search for biosignatures on exoplanets. Even scientists who reject strong Gaia credit it with provoking productive research into planetary feedbacks.

working.text: treat life and its physical environment as one interacting system rather than as separate domains studied in isolation.
explain any self-regulation through ordinary selection and feedback, as Daisyworld does, not through planetary foresight.
expect a mix of stabilising and destabilising couplings, since neither pure Gaian stability nor pure Medean self-destruction is fully correct.

limits: The strong, optimising version was heavily criticised by evolutionary biologists. W. Ford Doolittle argued nothing in any organism's genome could encode planet-wide feedback, and Richard Dawkins objected that global self-regulation would require organisms to act in concert with foresight, and that with no reproducing population of planets undergoing selection there is no way to build planetary-scale adaptation. These critiques target the teleological reading; a naturalistic, non-teleological Gaia is now influential in Earth system science while the purposive version is rejected. Some cited evidence, such as the CLAW cloud-feedback hypothesis, is itself contested and largely unsupported as originally stated.
misreadings: It does not require the Earth to be a literally conscious or living organism; the living-planet language is a metaphor, and taken literally corresponds to the discredited strong version, which is why Lovelock preferred geophysiology. It is not New Age mysticism, despite the mythological name; the core naturalistic claim is a testable one about feedback and stability. And it does not claim the Earth optimises conditions for humans or maintains stability deliberately.
origin: Formulated by the scientist James Lovelock from the 1960s, the name suggested by the novelist William Golding, developed with the microbiologist Lynn Margulis, and set out in 'Gaia: A New Look at Life on Earth' (1979).

sources.text: Gaia hypothesis, Wikipedia. — the self-regulating-system claim, the weak-to-strong spectrum, and the Doolittle and Dawkins critiques.
Watson and Lovelock, 'Biological homeostasis of the global environment: the parable of Daisyworld,' Tellus B 35 (1983): 284-289. — the model showing regulation without teleology.
